definition: A model of a system that is always in exactly one of a fixed, finite set of states and moves between them in response to inputs. Vending machines, traffic lights, protocol handlers and lexers are commonly designed this way.
example: A traffic light cycles through the states green, amber and red as its timer fires.

definition: A finite-state machine used to decide whether an input string belongs to a language: it reads the string one symbol at a time and finishes in an accepting or non-accepting state. DFAs and NFAs are the two standard kinds. "Automata" is the plural.
example: A 2-state finite automaton can decide whether a binary string contains an even number of 1s.

definition: A finite automaton with exactly one next state for every state and input symbol, so each input has a single run. It is described by a 5-tuple: states, alphabet, transition function, start state and accepting states. It decides membership in one pass with constant memory.
example: The 3-state DFA that tracks the remainder mod 3 accepts the binary string 1001 (nine).

definition: A finite automaton whose transition function can give several next states, or none, for a state and symbol, and may also allow ε-transitions that read no input. It accepts a string if at least one possible run ends in an accepting state. Every NFA has an equivalent DFA.
example: A 4-state NFA recognises "third symbol from the end is 1", while the smallest DFA needs 8 states.

definition: An NFA that is allowed ε-transitions: moves that change state without reading an input symbol. Thompson's construction produces ε-NFAs, and the subset construction removes the ε-moves when converting to a DFA.

One of the finitely many situations a finite automaton can be in. The current state is the only memory the automaton has, so it must summarise everything about the input read so far that matters for the future.
example: The parity DFA has two states, E (even number of 1s so far) and O (odd).

definition: The finite set of symbols an automaton can read, usually written Σ (capital Greek sigma). Strings and languages are always defined over an alphabet.
example: For binary strings the alphabet is {0, 1}; for many lesson examples it is {a, b}.

definition: A finite sequence of symbols taken from an alphabet. Its length is the number of symbols in it, and the empty string has length 0. In formal language theory a string is also called a word.
example: 0110 is a string of length 4 over the alphabet {0, 1}.

definition: The unique string with no symbols, of length 0, written ε (Greek epsilon). It is "" in Python. It belongs to a language only if the language explicitly includes it.
example: An automaton accepts the empty string exactly when its start state is accepting.

definition: The operation written *: R* matches zero or more copies of R joined together, and Σ* is the set of every finite string over the alphabet Σ, including the empty string. It is one of the three core regular-expression operations, with union and concatenation.
example: a* matches the empty string, a, aa, aaa and so on.

definition: Any set of strings over an alphabet; it may be finite or infinite. The language of an automaton is the set of strings it accepts, and the language of a regex is the set of strings it matches.
example: "Binary strings with an even number of 1s" is an infinite formal language over {0, 1}.

definition: The question "is this particular string in this language?". A DFA answers it for a regular language in one left-to-right pass over the string.
An ordered list of exactly five components. A DFA or NFA is formally the 5-tuple (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F): states, alphabet, transition function, start state and accepting states.
The rule, written δ (Greek delta), that says where an automaton goes next. For a DFA, δ(q, c) is the single next state from state q on symbol c; for an NFA it is a set of possible next states.
example: In the parity DFA, δ(E, 1) = O and δ(E, 0) = E.

definition: The function written δ̂ ("delta hat") that applies the transition function once per symbol of a whole string: δ̂(q, w) is the state reached by starting in q and reading all of w. For the empty string it returns q unchanged.
The state, written q₀, in which an automaton begins every run before reading any input.

A state in the automaton's set F of accepting (final) states. A DFA accepts a string if the run ends in one; an NFA accepts if at least one run ends in one. Diagrams mark them with a double circle or double brackets.
A table listing, for every state (row) and input symbol (column), the next state. It is the usual way to store a DFA in code, where running the machine is one table lookup per symbol.
A non-accepting state that loops to itself on every symbol, so once a run enters it the string can never be accepted. A missing arrow in a partial DFA implicitly means "go to the dead state".
example: In the decimal-number DFA, reading a second dot sends the run to the dead state.

definition: A DFA drawn with some transitions missing; each missing transition implicitly leads to a dead state. It must be completed before operations such as complementing.
A DFA whose transition function is total: it has a next state for every (state, symbol) pair. Complementing by swapping accepting and non-accepting states only works on a complete DFA.

A way to run two DFAs in parallel as one DFA whose states are pairs of states, one from each machine. Choosing which pairs accept gives the intersection, union, difference or symmetric difference of the two languages. The state count is the product of the two machines' state counts.
example: A 2-state and a 3-state DFA give a product with 2 × 3 = 6 states.

definition: A language that some finite automaton recognises; equivalently, one that some regular expression describes (Kleene's theorem). Regular languages can only need a bounded amount of memory to recognise, so "n a's followed by n b's" is not regular.
example: Binary numbers divisible by 3 form a regular language; balanced brackets of any depth do not.

definition: A class of languages is closed under an operation if applying the operation to languages in the class always gives a language in the class. Regular languages are closed under union, intersection, complement, concatenation, star and reversal.
example: If L is regular, so is L ∩ a*b*, which is the basis of many non-regularity proofs.

definition: The first stage of a compiler or interpreter, which splits source text into tokens such as identifiers, numbers and operators. Lexers are usually built from finite automata, one pattern per token type.
example: A lexer turns x = 42 into the tokens identifier, equals sign and number.

definition: A tool that takes token patterns written as regular expressions and generates lexer code, typically by building an NFA, determinising it to a DFA and emitting a transition table or code.
example: lex, flex and re2c are lexer generators.

definition: lex is a classic Unix lexer generator from the 1970s; flex (fast lexical analyser generator) is its widely used open-source successor. Both compile regular-expression token rules into a table-driven DFA in C.
An open-source lexer generator for C and other languages that compiles regular expressions into a DFA emitted as direct code rather than tables, minimising the DFA first.

A program component that checks the structure of input, such as source code, JSON or HTTP messages, and usually builds a tree from it. Parsers for nested structure need more than a finite automaton, typically a stack.

aliases: American Standard Code for Information Interchange
definition: A 7-bit character encoding with 128 codes, covering English letters, the digits 0 to 9, punctuation and control characters. It is the first 128 code points of Unicode.
example: The ASCII digits 0 to 9 have codes 48 to 57.

definition: The standard that assigns a number (code point) to characters from almost every writing system, with well over 150,000 characters. A Unicode character class like \w covers far more characters than ASCII, which makes compiled automata much larger.
Software or hardware that inspects network packets and allows or drops them according to rules on fields such as addresses and ports. Many are implemented as state machines.
A digital circuit whose state elements all update together on the edges of a shared clock signal. Its stored bits form a finite state, so it can be modelled as a finite-state machine.
A drawing of a finite-state machine: circles for states and labelled arrows for transitions, with the start state marked by an arrow from nowhere and accepting states by double circles.
The automated step in hardware design that turns a description of behaviour, such as a state machine, into a network of logic gates and flip-flops.

Artificial intelligence: software that makes decisions or behaves in ways that seem intelligent. In games, "AI" usually means the logic controlling non-player characters, often written as a state machine.
User interface: the screens, controls and flows through which a person uses software. Multi-step UI flows are often modelled as state machines.

A yes-or-no question about inputs is decidable if some algorithm always halts with the correct answer. For DFAs, questions such as "is the language empty?" and "are these two DFAs equivalent?" are decidable.
A finite automaton extended with a stack, an unbounded last-in-first-out memory. The extra memory lets it recognise nested structures like balanced brackets, which no finite automaton can.

A way to build a DFA for "binary numbers divisible by k": one state per remainder 0 to k − 1, and on reading bit b, move from remainder r to (2r + b) mod k. It uses k states, though some may merge after minimisation.
example: For k = 3, reading 1001 goes through remainders 0, 1, 2, 1, 0 and accepts.

definition: The leftmost bit of a binary number, the one with the greatest place value. Reading "most significant bit first" means reading the number left to right.
example: In 1001 (nine) the most significant bit is worth 8.

definition: In automata, the ability to have several possible moves at once. A nondeterministic machine accepts if any choice of moves leads to acceptance: it is an existence statement, not randomness.
An NFA move that changes state without reading any input symbol, labelled ε (the empty string). ε-transitions make it easy to glue automata together; a loop made only of them is an ε-cycle.

The ε-closure of a set of NFA states is that set plus every state reachable from it by following only ε-transitions. NFA simulation and the subset construction take the closure at the start and after every symbol.
example: If 1 has ε-arrows to 2 and 2 to 3, the ε-closure of {1} is {1, 2, 3}.

definition: The algorithm that converts an NFA into an equivalent DFA whose states are sets of NFA states. An m-state NFA gives at most 2^m DFA states; usually only reachable sets are built.
example: For "ends in ab", only 3 of the 8 possible subsets of the 3 NFA states are reachable.

definition: The 1959 result by Michael Rabin and Dana Scott that nondeterministic finite automata recognise exactly the same languages as deterministic ones, proved with the subset construction. Their paper, which introduced nondeterministic machines, earned them the 1976 Turing Award.
Every state has at most a fixed number of outgoing arrows. Thompson NFAs have at most two per state, so the number of transitions is proportional to the number of states.
Running several processes so that each takes its next step at the same moment as the others. NFA simulation runs all possible paths in lockstep, one input symbol at a time.

A DFA built on demand during matching: each new set of NFA states and its transitions are computed the first time the input reaches them, then cached. Engines bound the cache and clear it or fall back to NFA simulation if it fills.
example: RE2 and Rust's regex use a lazy DFA as a fast path.

definition: A pattern describing a set of strings. Formally it is built from ∅, ε and single symbols using union (|), concatenation and Kleene star (*); everyday regex syntax adds shorthand such as +, ? and character classes, and some engines add non-regular features like backreferences.
example: (a|b)*abb matches every string of a's and b's that ends in abb.

definition: The library code that compiles a regular expression and searches text with it. Engines either backtrack through the pattern (Perl, PCRE, Python, Java) or simulate an automaton (RE2, Go, Rust), with very different worst-case costs.

Google's open-source C++ regex library, designed to run in time linear in the input for its supported syntax by simulating automata instead of backtracking. It omits backreferences and lookaround. RE2/J is its Java port and google-re2 its Python binding.
The regular expression package in the Go standard library. Its documentation guarantees matching in time linear in the size of the input, using RE2 syntax and automaton-based methods.
The main regular expression library for the Rust language. It guarantees O(m · n) worst-case time for a single search (pattern size m, input length n) and omits backreferences and lookaround.

Ken Thompson's 1968 method for compiling a regular expression into an ε-NFA by building a small fragment per symbol or operator and gluing fragments with ε-transitions. The NFA has at most about two states per symbol or operator, so it is linear in the regex size. Thompson's paper also matched text by simulating that NFA, tracking the set of active states.
example: (a|b)*abb becomes a 14-state NFA in the lesson's version.

definition: American computer scientist who co-created Unix and the B language, wrote the ed editor and the original grep, published Thompson's construction in 1968 and later co-designed Go.
Stephen Kleene's 1956 result that regular expressions and finite automata describe exactly the same class of languages, the regular languages.
American mathematician (1909–1994) who founded much of recursion theory and introduced regular expressions and the star operation named after him.

Joining strings end to end: the concatenation of ab and ba is abba. For regexes, RS matches a string of R followed by a string of S. It is written by placing items side by side, sometimes with an explicit dot.
The regex operator |, meaning "either side": R|S matches anything R matches or anything S matches. It is the regex form of language union and has the lowest precedence.
example: ab|c* means (ab)|(c*).

definition: Notation that makes something easier to write without adding power, because it can be rewritten in terms of more basic constructs.
example: In regexes, R+ is sugar for RR*.

definition: The regex symbol . that matches any single character. Most engines exclude the newline character unless a dot-all (single-line) option is turned on.

A regex feature such as \1 that must match exactly the same text as an earlier capture group. General backreferences let patterns describe non-regular languages, so automaton-based engines like RE2 do not support them.
example: (\w+) \1 matches a repeated word such as "the the".

definition: The rule for which operators bind tighter when no brackets are given. In regexes, star binds tightest, then concatenation, then union.
example: ^ab|cd$ means (^ab)|(cd$), not ^(ab|cd)$.

definition: In Thompson's construction, the small NFA built for one part of the regex. Each has exactly one start state with no incoming arrows and one accepting state with no outgoing arrows, so fragments can be glued safely.
Writing each operator after its operands, so no brackets are needed and a stack can evaluate it left to right. Ordinary notation with operators between operands is called infix.
example: The infix regex (a|b)*abb becomes ab|*a.b.b. in postfix.

definition: Edsger Dijkstra's algorithm for converting infix expressions to postfix using a stack of operators and their precedences.
A last-in-first-out data structure: you push items on top and pop the most recent one off. Parsers, Thompson's construction and backtracking engines all use stacks.
The nickname of Compilers: Principles, Techniques, and Tools by Aho, Lam, Sethi and Ullman, the classic compiler textbook, named after the dragon on its cover.

A method for converting an automaton into an equivalent regular expression by removing states one at a time and relabelling the arrows that bypassed them with regexes. The result can be exponentially long.

A way of simulating a Thompson NFA, compiled as a small program of match, split and jump instructions, in which each active thread also carries capture-group positions. Named after Rob Pike; used by RE2, Go and Rust.
An NFA built from a regex with no ε-transitions and one state per symbol occurrence plus a start state. Its regular shape suits bit-parallel matching.
The derivative of a regex with respect to a symbol is a regex for what remains to be matched after reading that symbol. Repeatedly taking derivatives builds a DFA directly from a regex.
Matching that stores the set of active automaton states as bits of a machine word and updates them all at once with bitwise operations.
Regex syntax such as R{2,5} or R{1000} that repeats R a given number of times. Automaton engines expand it into copies, so a large count makes a large automaton; RE2 rejects counts over 1000.
Regex syntax such as [a-z] or \d that matches any one character from a set. Formally it is a union of single symbols.
A bracketed part of a regex whose matched text is recorded so the program, or a backreference, can use it.
example: Matching (\d+)-(\d+) against 10-20 captures 10 and 20.

definition: A search that tries one choice, continues, and on failure returns to the most recent choice point to try another. Perl-style regex engines backtrack through the pattern, which can take exponential time on ambiguous patterns.
Regular expression denial of service: an attack or accident in which a crafted input makes a backtracking regex engine take exponential or polynomial time, tying up the CPU.
example: Matching (a+)+$ against 30 a's and a ! can explore hundreds of millions of paths.

definition: A regex is ambiguous when some text can be matched by several different paths through it. Ambiguity under repetition is what makes backtracking engines blow up.
example: (a|a)* can match each a with either branch.

definition: A quantifier is a regex repetition operator such as *, + or {n}. Nested regex quantifiers put one inside another, as in (a+)+, which lets a run of characters be split among iterations in exponentially many ways.
Regex assertions such as (?=...) and (?<=...) that check what follows or precedes the current position without consuming it. RE2, Go and Rust's regex do not support them.
A regex group written (?>...) that, once it has matched, never gives back characters when later parts fail. It removes some backtracking but can change which strings match. Python added it in 3.11.
example: (?>a*)a can never match, because the group keeps every a.

definition: A quantifier with an extra +, such as a*+ or a++, that matches as much as it can and never gives any back, like an atomic group around a greedy quantifier.
example: a*+a behaves like (?>a*)a.

definition: A fast substring search for a fixed string that every match must contain, run before the full regex so that the automaton only runs near likely matches.
example: For ERROR.*timeout, first search for ERROR.

definition: The Perl-style rule for which match a regex reports: the earliest starting position, and among matches there, the one preferred by the order of alternatives and greediness.
A match forced to start or end at a fixed place, such as the start of the text (^) or the end ($). An unanchored search may begin at any position, which can multiply the work.
Web application firewall: a filter in front of web applications that inspects HTTP requests against rules, often regexes, and blocks suspicious ones.
A company running a large global CDN, reverse proxy and security network. A badly behaved WAF regex took its proxy and CDN down for 27 minutes on 2 July 2019.
A limit on how long an operation may run before it is abandoned. .NET regexes accept a match timeout; Python's re and Java's java.util.regex have none built in.
A tool that feeds large numbers of generated or mutated inputs to a program to find crashes, hangs or very slow cases.
A tool that inspects code or patterns without running them, looking for bugs; ReDoS analysers flag regexes with exponential ambiguity.

Perl Compatible Regular Expressions: a widely used C regex library implementing Perl syntax with a backtracking matcher. PCRE2 is its current version and also offers a separate DFA-style matching function.
A scripting language, first released in 1987, whose rich regex syntax (backreferences, lookaround, lazy quantifiers) became the model for most modern backtracking engines.

Microsoft's software platform for languages such as C#. Its Regex class backtracks by default; since .NET 7, RegexOptions.NonBacktracking selects a linear-time engine that does not allow backreferences, lookarounds, atomic groups or balancing groups.
The regex package in the Java standard library. It uses a backtracking matcher and has no built-in match timeout.
Python's standard regex module. It uses a backtracking matcher, has no built-in timeout, and from Python 3.11 supports atomic groups and possessive quantifiers.
example: re.fullmatch("ab|c*", "cc") succeeds.

definition: Google's JavaScript engine, used in Chrome and Node.js. Its team described an experimental non-backtracking regex engine in 2021.
The Unix command-line tool that prints lines matching a regular expression. GNU grep picks among DFA-based, literal-search and other matching strategies depending on the pattern and options.
GNU's Not Unix: the free-software project that produced many standard Unix-like tools, including GNU grep and GCC.
HyperText Markup Language: the nested tag language of web pages. Its arbitrarily deep nesting is beyond what a regex can parse.

A property every regular language has: there is a pumping length p such that every string in the language of length at least p has a non-empty piece within its first p symbols that can be repeated any number of times, or deleted, without leaving the language. Showing a language lacks this property proves it is not regular. Context-free languages have their own, different pumping lemma.
example: For n a's followed by n b's, pumping a block of a's from the first p symbols unbalances the counts, so that language is not regular.

definition: The number p in a pumping lemma: strings at least this long are guaranteed to contain a piece that can be pumped. For the regular-language lemma, the number of states of a DFA recognising the language works. In a proof you must keep p as an unknown, because the adversary chooses it.
A string that reads the same forwards and backwards, such as abba or aabaa. The palindromes over two symbols form a non-regular language.
A whole number that is another whole number times itself: 0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, and so on.

The theorem, proved by John Myhill and Anil Nerode in 1957, that a language is regular exactly when its L-equivalence relation has finitely many classes, and that the number of classes is the number of states in the minimal DFA. It gives an exact test for regularity.

Two strings are L-equivalent if every possible suffix gives the same verdict for both: both completed strings are in L or both are not. Each equivalence class corresponds to one state of the minimal DFA.
example: For "ends in ab", the strings a and bba are L-equivalent.

definition: Two states (or two strings) are distinguishable if some suffix makes exactly one of them reach acceptance. States that are not distinguishable are equivalent and can be merged.
Two DFA states are equivalent if every possible remaining input leads both to acceptance or both to rejection. Merging equivalent states never changes the language.
A string that, appended to two prefixes or read from two states, is accepted in one case and rejected in the other, proving the two must be kept apart.
example: The suffix b distinguishes states A and D in the lesson's example.

definition: The DFA with the fewest states for a given language. For a complete DFA over a fixed alphabet it is unique up to renaming states, so it serves as a canonical form.
Turning a DFA into the minimal DFA for the same language by deleting unreachable states and merging equivalent ones. Algorithms include Moore's, table filling, Hopcroft's and Brzozowski's.
A standard representation such that two objects are equivalent exactly when their standard representations are identical. The minimal DFA is a canonical form for regular languages.
Identical except for the names given to the parts. Two minimal DFAs for the same language are the same machine up to renaming of states.
A state that no input can reach from the start state. It cannot affect the language, so minimisation deletes it.

An algorithm style that starts with a coarse division of items into blocks and repeatedly splits blocks whose members behave differently, until no block splits. DFA minimisation starts from accepting versus non-accepting states.

In partition refinement, a division into blocks where every member of each block moves to the same blocks on every symbol, so no further split is possible. Its blocks are the states of the minimal DFA.
In the lesson's Python minimiser, a tuple of a state's current block and the blocks it moves to on each symbol. States with equal signatures stay in the same block for the next round.

Edward F. Moore's partition-refinement method for DFA minimisation: split accepting from non-accepting states, then repeatedly split blocks by where their members go. Worst case O(k n²) for n states and k symbols.

A DFA minimisation method that marks distinguishable pairs of states in a triangular table: first pairs differing in acceptance, then any pair whose successors on some symbol are already marked. Unmarked pairs are equivalent.
John Hopcroft's 1971 DFA minimisation algorithm, which refines partitions using a worklist and schedules only the smaller half of each split. It runs in O(k n log n) for n states and k symbols.
Janusz Brzozowski's minimisation method: reverse the automaton, determinise, reverse again and determinise again. The result is always minimal, but an intermediate step can be exponentially large.
Flipping every arrow of an automaton and swapping its start and accepting states. The result recognises every string of the original language written backwards.
A queue or stack of items still waiting to be processed by an algorithm. Hopcroft's algorithm keeps a worklist of blocks to split by.
The automaton obtained by merging each block of equivalent states into a single state. For a stable partition it is the minimal DFA.

Dana Angluin's 1987 algorithm that learns the minimal DFA of an unknown regular language by asking membership queries and equivalence queries. It is used to infer models of black-box protocols and software.
In automata learning, a question to a teacher of the form "is this string in the language?".
In automata learning, a question "is this hypothesis automaton correct?", answered yes or with a counterexample string.
A system studied only through its inputs and outputs, without seeing its internals.

PSPACE is the class of problems solvable using an amount of memory polynomial in the input size. A PSPACE-complete problem is among the hardest in that class; none is known to have a polynomial-time algorithm. Minimising an NFA is PSPACE-complete.
Breadth-first search: exploring a graph level by level, visiting everything one step away before anything two steps away. Searching a product automaton breadth-first finds a shortest counterexample.
Exploring a graph by following one path as far as possible before backing up to try the next. A backtracking regex engine walks the NFA depth-first.
Growth by a constant factor per step, such as doubling for each extra input character: 2ⁿ for n characters. It quickly becomes unmanageable: 2³⁰ is over a billion.
example: The subset construction can turn a 21-state NFA into a DFA with 2²⁰, about a million, states.

definition: Work that grows with the square of the input size, so doubling the input roughly quadruples the work.
Work that grows with the cube of the input size, so doubling the input multiplies the work by about 8.
Describing behaviour as the input size grows without limit, ignoring constant factors and small inputs. Big O bounds are asymptotic.
The input of a given size that makes an algorithm do the most work. A worst-case bound holds for every input.
Extra memory an algorithm uses beyond its input and fixed data. A DFA needs only O(1) auxiliary space: the current state.
A unit of data, 1,000,000 bytes in SI usage (sometimes used loosely for 1,048,576 bytes).
example: A 1 MB log file holds about a million characters.

definition: A unit of data, 1,000,000,000 bytes in SI usage.
Running an NFA by keeping the set of all states it could currently be in and updating that set once per input symbol. It never backtracks and takes O(m) work per symbol for an m-state Thompson NFA.
The part of a program that runs most often, such as code executed on every web request, where slowness matters most.
The sum 1 + 2 + … + n, which equals n(n + 1)/2: roughly half of n squared.
A large question-and-answer website for programmers, cited as one example of a regex-related outage.
A precise mathematical description of a kind of computer and what it can do, used to reason about what is computable and at what cost. Finite automata are the simplest useful one.
The lexer rule that each token is the longest prefix of the remaining input matching some token pattern. Implementing it may require reading ahead and backing up.
A .NET regex feature that pushes and pops captures like a stack, letting patterns match nested brackets beyond formal regular expressions.
A DFA in which every state is reachable from the start state.
A language over a one-symbol alphabet such as {a}, where a string is described entirely by its length.
Software engineer who wrote RE2 and Go's regexp package and a widely read series of articles explaining automaton-based regex matching.
The amount of work done per unit of time, such as megabytes of text scanned per second.
Marking a character so it is treated literally rather than as an operator, usually with a backslash: \. matches a real dot.
A dynamic programming language. Ruby 3.2 added memoization to its regex engine to prevent many cases of excessive backtracking.
The programming language of web browsers. Its standard regex engines backtrack.

A systems programming language focused on memory safety without garbage collection. Its main regex library, the regex crate maintained by the Rust project (not part of the standard library itself), is automaton based.

A regex engine that simulates a finite automaton, by tracking sets of states, a Pike VM or a lazy DFA, instead of backtracking. RE2, Go regexp and Rust regex work this way and guarantee time linear in the input for a fixed pattern.

In a pumping-lemma proof viewed as a game, the opponent who claims the language is regular. The adversary chooses the pumping length and how to split your string, so your argument must work for every choice they could make.

In a pumping-lemma proof, the part of the chosen string that is repeated or deleted. In the regular-language lemma it is y in x · y · z, must be non-empty, and lies within the first p symbols; the context-free lemma has two pumped pieces, v and y.
example: For aaabbb with pumping length 3, any pumped piece is a block of a's such as aa.
